links: workloads now run on the platform, and losing a site would still mean rebuilding them by hand
databases already run on the platform, but are still provisioned, patched and copied by hand
point-in-time recovery protects a database, not the site it runs on
immutable copies need a target that an administrator cannot delete from
a platform run by hand caps how many clusters one team can look after
databases are the request teams wait longest for, and the first catalog item worth automating
the same platform at the sites removes a second set of skills and tools
a site's copy at the core is what brings it back after a disaster

hci.label: Platform (hyperconverged)
hci.description: Hyperconverged infrastructure and private cloud: clusters that run virtual machines, storage and networking together, with protection, recovery and lifecycle to adopt.

questions.q: What does an hour of downtime cost on your most important application?
questions.why: Turns recovery features into money the sponsor recognises.
questions.need: The cost of an hour down on the key application is known
questions.how: Put a number on it with the application owner
questions.listen: A number with an owner is a business case. 'It would be bad' means nobody has counted it yet: count it with them.
questions.probe: Who would notice first, a customer or an internal team, and how long before it reached the board?

questions.q: When did you last restore a whole system, not a file, and how long did it take?
questions.why: Untested recovery is the usual gap behind a confident answer.
questions.need: A whole system can be restored in a known time
questions.how: Restore one complete system and time it
questions.listen: Never, or not end to end, is the gap. A timed test in the last quarter is a strength to build on.
questions.probe: What was slower than planned in that restore, and who was waiting for it?

questions.q: How many clusters run outside the main data centre: plants, branches, edge sites?
questions.why: Remote clusters are the ones the central console does not see.
questions.need: Clusters outside the main data centre are known and managed
questions.how: Bring plant, branch and edge clusters under central management
questions.listen: Sites with no local IT staff are where a platform that looks after itself pays most.
questions.probe: How is a failed disk at the furthest site replaced today, and how long does it take?

questions.q: Do you know which virtual machines have no owner and what they run?
questions.why: Unowned machines are skipped by protection and patching.
questions.need: Every virtual machine has an owner and a purpose
questions.how: Tag machines with owners and retire the orphans
questions.listen: If nobody can say, the estate is bigger than it needs to be: the first saving is what can be switched off.
questions.probe: When did anyone last switch off a machine nobody claimed, and what happened?

questions.q: Which workloads have snapshots, and could an administrator account delete them?
questions.why: Snapshots an attacker can delete are not ransomware protection.
questions.need: Important workloads have snapshots that an admin cannot delete
questions.how: Apply protection policies with immutable copies
questions.listen: Yes, or 'not sure', means one stolen account can erase the safety net.
questions.probe: Who holds those administrator accounts, and does deleting a copy need a second person?

questions.q: Is there a second site, and has failover to it been run end to end?
questions.why: Replication without a tested recovery plan is a hope.
questions.need: Failover to a second site has been run end to end
questions.how: Run a test failover of one application
questions.listen: A runbook that has never been run end to end is a hope, not a plan.
questions.probe: What would you rather the auditor did not see in your last failover test?

questions.q: How far behind on upgrades are you, and what makes upgrading hard?
questions.why: Lifecycle debt is a security risk and the most common hidden effort.
questions.need: Upgrades are routine, not a project
questions.how: Agree an upgrade cadence and remove what makes upgrading hard
questions.listen: Upgrades planned around weekends and change boards cost people every time: that time is the saving.
questions.probe: How many people and nights did the last full upgrade take: firmware, hypervisor and storage?

questions.q: When the platform raises an alert at night, who acts on it?
questions.why: Alerts without an owner turn into noise, then into outages.
questions.need: A platform alert at night reaches someone who acts
questions.how: Route platform alerts to a named on-call owner
questions.listen: A named person with a runbook is mature. 'The supplier calls us', or nobody, means outages last longer than they should.
questions.probe: Which alert last woke someone up, and was it worth it?

questions.q: Which failures must the platform ride through without stopping: a disk, a server, a whole rack, a room?
questions.why: The answer decides how many copies of the data are kept and where they are placed.
questions.need: The failures to survive are agreed, and every copy of the data sits in a different place for each of them
questions.how: Agree the failure domains (server, rack, room) and how many copies each group of workloads needs
questions.listen: This decides how many copies of the data to keep and how much headroom to buy: write it down as a requirement.
questions.probe: Has a whole rack or room ever failed, and what stopped with it?

questions.q: How full are storage and hosts today, and how much room is kept free for a server failure and for growth?
questions.why: A platform run at the edge cannot rebuild after a failure, and the next purchase arrives as an emergency.
questions.need: Capacity is planned with room to rebuild after a failure and to grow, with alerts before it runs short
questions.how: Measure today's use, keep a server's worth of room free, and set alerts at two thresholds
questions.listen: Above about three quarters full, a server failure can leave no room to rebuild: a sizing input, not a detail.
questions.probe: How fast has used capacity grown over the last two years?

questions.q: Which workloads need the fastest storage, and which can live on cheaper capacity?
questions.why: Separating hot from cold data, and deciding where to compress or deduplicate, is where cost and performance are won.
questions.need: Workloads are grouped by the performance they need, with data reduction used where it pays off
questions.how: Group workloads by performance tier and agree where compression and deduplication apply
questions.listen: A few latency-sensitive systems often drive the whole design: name them now so the proof measures them.
questions.probe: Which application owner complains first when storage slows down?

questions.q: Could a tested platform update be pre-approved as routine and run during the working day?
questions.why: Updates that need a weekend get postponed, and a platform that falls behind becomes a risk.
questions.need: Tested platform updates are pre-approved and run during the working day, without downtime
questions.how: Agree with change management a pre-approved path for tested updates
questions.listen: If every update needs a change board at night, simple rolling updates are worth hours a month: agree it as a goal.
questions.probe: What would the change board need to see to treat a tested update as a standard change?

questions.q: What hardware runs the estate today, how old is it, and when does its support end?
questions.why: The end of hardware support is often the real date behind the project.
questions.need: Servers and arrays are listed with their end-of-support dates
questions.how: Export the hardware list with purchase and support dates
questions.listen: An array or a server fleet out of support within 18 months is a reason to decide this year, with a date.
questions.probe: What would it cost to extend support on the oldest array for two more years?

questions.q: Is there a week of performance data for the estate, processor, memory, storage and network, covering the busiest days?
questions.why: Sizing on what machines are given rather than what they use over-buys; a week of peaks sizes it right.
questions.need: A week of performance data covers the busiest days
questions.how: Run a collector for seven days that include month-end or the busiest day
questions.listen: Without measured peaks, sizing falls back on what was allocated, often several times what is used.
questions.probe: Which days of the month are the busiest, and can the collection include one?

questions.q: How much storage belongs to machines that are switched off, and do they still need it?
questions.why: Switched-off machines still hold data: it must be sized, or retired.
questions.need: Switched-off machines are either sized or retired
questions.how: List switched-off machines with their storage and an owner's decision
questions.listen: A large share of switched-off capacity is an early win: retire it before buying for it.
questions.probe: Who can approve retiring a machine that has been off for six months?

questions.q: Which software is licensed per processor core or per host, and does that shape how servers are built?
questions.why: Database and operating system licences can cost more than the platform; they decide the processor choice.
questions.need: Per-core licences are known and the design keeps them on the fewest cores
questions.how: List per-core licences and the hosts they are tied to
questions.listen: Per-core software calls for fewer, faster cores on dedicated hosts. Ignoring it can erase the savings.
questions.probe: What did the last licence true-up or audit cost, and for which product?

questions.q: Which data must be encrypted at rest, and where are encryption keys managed today?
questions.why: Encryption and key management are often a gate in the security review.
questions.need: Encryption at rest and the key manager are agreed with security
questions.how: Ask security for the policy on encryption at rest and key management
questions.listen: A key manager already in place is a requirement to test in the proof, not a footnote.
questions.probe: Who approves a new system that holds encrypted data, and how long does that review take?

questions.q: How many people run the infrastructure, and what would they do with the time if routine work went away?
questions.why: The value of simpler operations is the work it frees, said by the team itself.
questions.need: The team's routine hours are known, and where freed time would go
questions.how: List the routine tasks of a typical month with their hours
questions.listen: A named project waiting for those hours makes the saving real. 'Nothing' means it will not be believed.
questions.probe: Which project was postponed this year for lack of people?

proof.text: A virtual machine is restored from an immutable snapshot after a simulated ransomware encryption
proof.how: Encrypt a test VM's disk, try to delete its snapshots as an administrator, then restore it and time the restore.

proof.text: A planned failover to the secondary site meets the agreed recovery time and recovery point
proof.how: Run the recovery plan on a test application and record the time to service and the data lost.

proof.text: A host fails and its virtual machines restart elsewhere with no manual step
proof.how: Power off one node during a load test and watch the workloads move.

proof.text: A full software and firmware upgrade completes on a running cluster with no workload downtime
proof.how: Upgrade a cluster carrying a test workload and check that it never stops serving.

proof.text: A new virtual machine is provisioned by an application team through self-service within its quota
proof.how: Have one team request and receive a VM without opening a ticket.

proof.text: The capacity forecast names the month the cluster runs out of storage, and the team agrees with it
proof.how: Compare the forecast with the team's own estimate and growth plan.

proof.text: After a server is lost, the platform rebuilds every missing copy on its own, and the time it took is recorded
proof.how: Power off a server under load, watch the rebuild complete without operator action, and note its duration

proof.text: Performance is tested with many machines and disks at once, against the current platform's baseline and a pass mark agreed beforehand
proof.how: Run the customer's own load test, not one machine with one disk, and compare with the baseline

readiness: IP addresses agreed: per server for the host, the platform's controller and out-of-band management, plus a cluster address and a data services address
DNS and NTP reachable from every server
Switch ports, VLANs and uplinks agreed with the network team, with two switches for redundancy
The servers in the test checked against the platform's supported hardware list
Test workloads chosen, with their owners, and a way to generate load
The failures to test agreed: a disk, a server, a network link
If existing storage arrays are to be used: their model and software version, and the servers' boot devices, checked against the supported list

audiences.executive: One platform for every application, run by a smaller team, that grows a server at a time instead of in a refresh every five years.
audiences.technical: Compute, storage and networking managed as one, upgraded without downtime, with protection and security set by policy.
audiences.financial: Capacity bought when it is needed, not years ahead; fewer tools and contracts to renew; hardware still supported stays in use.

people: The infrastructure lead who runs the current platform
The storage and network owners, whose work changes
An application owner with a workload to test
Whoever signs the next refresh or renewal

objections.says: This is fine for small sites, not for our core applications.
objections.clarify: Which applications, and what do they need: latency, throughput, capacity?
objections.answer: Agree the numbers that matter for those applications and test them, rather than argue about architecture.
objections.prove: Run the agreed workload mix, many machines and disks at once, against the current platform's baseline.

objections.says: The platform's own services take resources away from our workloads.
objections.clarify: Is the concern resources reserved, resources actually used, or licences counted on them?
objections.answer: Separate what is allocated from what is consumed, and size with the platform's own services counted from the start.
objections.prove: Measure consumption under the agreed load and compare the usable capacity with the sizing sketch.

objections.says: We have just bought new storage arrays.
objections.clarify: Until when are they supported, and which workloads must stay on them?
objections.answer: Keep them where they still make sense: compute can move first, and data can follow when the arrays reach the end of support.
objections.prove: Run test machines on the new platform with their disks still on the existing array, at the agreed performance.

objections.says: Our storage team would have nothing left to do.
objections.clarify: Is this about people, skills, or control over data protection?
objections.answer: Their work moves from looking after arrays to setting protection, capacity and recovery policies for the whole platform.
objections.prove: Have the storage team run a restore and a capacity forecast themselves during the test.

dr-backup.label: Disaster recovery and backup
dr-backup.description: Disaster recovery and backup: sites whose workloads must be copied, recoverable within agreed times, and tested before they are needed.

questions.q: What would one day without your main site cost, and has anyone put a number on it?
questions.why: Turns recovery objectives into a business decision.
questions.need: The cost of a day without the main site is known and agreed
questions.how: Put a number on it with finance and the business owner
questions.listen: A figure per hour or per day turns recovery time into a budget line.
questions.probe: Which service would the business restore first, and has it agreed that order?

questions.q: When was the last full recovery test, and what went wrong in it?
questions.why: Tests always find something; no test means it is still hidden.
questions.need: A full recovery test runs regularly, and its findings are closed
questions.how: Schedule a non-disruptive test failover and track what it finds
questions.listen: No full test in the last year means every recovery time is a guess.
questions.probe: What did the test leave out because it was too risky or too hard?

questions.q: Which sites and branches have no copy of their workloads anywhere?
questions.why: Unprotected sites are the first gap to close.
questions.need: Every site and branch has a copy of its workloads
questions.how: Connect the unprotected sites and start their first copies
questions.listen: Branches with no copy are where one fire or one attack becomes permanent loss.
questions.probe: What would be lost for good if the smallest site burned down tonight?

questions.q: Has every workload been given a recovery point and a recovery time, agreed with the business?
questions.why: Without objectives, nothing can be checked or prioritised.
questions.need: Every workload has a recovery point and time agreed with the business
questions.how: Classify workloads in tiers with the business owners
questions.listen: Targets set by IT alone are wrong in both directions; agreed with the business they become a design input.
questions.probe: Which system has the strictest target, and who set it?

questions.q: Could an administrator account delete your backups today?
questions.why: If yes, ransomware can too.
questions.need: No administrator account can delete the backups
questions.how: Keep an immutable copy that admins cannot remove
questions.listen: If one account can delete the copies, so can ransomware: copies nobody can change, and a second approver, close it.
questions.probe: Is there a copy that no administrator can change before it expires?

questions.q: Does the recovery plan include the network: addresses, DNS, firewall rules?
questions.why: Most failed recoveries fail on the network, not on the data.
questions.need: The recovery plan includes the network
questions.how: Add addresses, DNS and firewall changes to the plan, and test them
questions.listen: Failovers fail on addresses, name resolution and firewall rules more often than on data.
questions.probe: Will machines keep their addresses at the recovery site, or be given new ones?

questions.q: Who can start a failover, and do they have the runbook at night?
questions.why: Recovery depends on people as much as on copies.
questions.need: Whoever starts a failover has the runbook, at night too
questions.how: Name who can start it, and give them a one-click plan
questions.listen: One named person with the runbook in hand saves the first hour of a disaster.
questions.probe: Who can declare a disaster when the head of IT cannot be reached?

questions.q: When a replication falls behind, who is told and what do they do?
questions.why: A silent missed recovery point is discovered on the worst day.
questions.need: A replication that falls behind reaches a named owner
questions.how: Alert on missed recovery points with an owner and a response
questions.listen: Silent lag is how a recovery point of minutes becomes hours on the day.
questions.probe: When did replication last fall behind, and how long before anyone noticed?

questions.q: Which workloads can lose no data at all, which can lose minutes, and which can lose hours?
questions.why: Zero, minutes and hours need different replication, distances and costs.
questions.need: Every workload sits in a recovery tier (zero, minutes, hours) with the replication that matches it
questions.how: Group workloads into recovery tiers with the business and pick the replication for each
questions.listen: Zero loss needs synchronous copies over short distances; minutes or hours cost far less. Sort systems into these tiers.
questions.probe: How many systems truly need zero data loss, if each had to justify the cost?

questions.q: How far back must you be able to go, and how close together must the recovery points be?
questions.why: Keeping every point forever costs storage; keeping too few loses the point you need after ransomware went unnoticed for days.
questions.need: Retention is agreed per tier: recent recovery points close together, older ones further apart
questions.how: Agree a retention scheme, for example hourly for a day, daily for a week, weekly for a month
questions.listen: An intruder may sit unnoticed for weeks: retention must reach further back than that.
questions.probe: How long could an intruder have been inside before your last incident or test found them?

questions.q: Which machines must come back together, in the same state and in a set order: an application with its database, say?
questions.why: Recovering machines one by one, from different moments, breaks applications that depend on each other.
questions.need: Applications that depend on each other are protected as a group and recovered in a set order
questions.how: Group dependent machines, snapshot each group together, and write the power-on order into the plan
questions.listen: Applications whose parts must return to the same instant need consistency groups and a set start order.
questions.probe: Which application has the most parts that must come back in order?

questions.q: Where is the second site, how far away, and what is the network round-trip time between them?
questions.why: Distance and latency decide whether copies can be synchronous.
questions.need: Distance and round-trip time between the sites are measured
questions.how: Measure round-trip time between the sites at peak
questions.listen: Under about five milliseconds allows zero-loss copies; beyond that, plan near-continuous or scheduled copies.
questions.probe: Is there a third place, a cloud or a partner site, that could hold a copy?

questions.q: How much data changes per day on the systems to protect, and how much bandwidth is there for replication?
questions.why: Daily change and bandwidth decide which recovery points are achievable.
questions.need: Daily change and replication bandwidth are known
questions.how: Measure daily change per protected system
questions.listen: If the link cannot carry a day's change within the recovery point, the target or the link must change.
questions.probe: Does replication share the link with users, and at which hours?

questions.q: Which backup software and storage are used today, and when do their contracts and support end?
questions.why: An existing backup stack can be kept, integrated or replaced: the dates decide which.
questions.need: The backup stack is listed with its contract dates
questions.how: List backup software, targets and renewal dates
questions.listen: A renewal in the same year as the platform decision is a chance to simplify both.
questions.probe: Which backup jobs fail most often, and why?

questions.q: Must recovery be tested regularly for an auditor or a regulation, and how is the test documented today?
questions.why: Required tests make automated, non-disruptive testing worth money.
questions.need: Recovery tests and their evidence meet what the auditor asks
questions.how: Ask compliance for the test frequency and the evidence required
questions.listen: A manual test once a year for the auditor costs weekends; one run monthly in an isolated network is the upgrade.
questions.probe: What did the last auditor ask for that took longest to produce?

questions.q: If ransomware struck tonight, where would you restore to, and how would you know the copy is clean?
questions.why: Recovering from ransomware needs a clean place and a known-good point, not only a copy.
questions.need: A clean recovery environment and a way to find the last good copy are planned
questions.how: Agree where a clean restore would run and how copies are checked
questions.listen: Restoring into the same infected network repeats the attack: an isolated recovery area is the requirement.
questions.probe: Who decides which copy is clean enough to restore, and on what evidence?

proof.text: A test failover of a business application meets the agreed recovery time and point, without touching production
proof.how: Run the recovery plan in test mode and record time to service and data lost.

proof.text: After a simulated ransomware attack, systems are restored from an immutable copy that the attacker's admin account could not delete
proof.how: Try to delete the copies with an administrator account, then restore from them.

proof.text: A missed recovery point raises an alert to a named owner within minutes
proof.how: Pause replication for one VM and watch who is told.

proof.text: A failback to the primary site completes in the order of the plan, with no manual network change
proof.how: Fail back the test application and check its addresses and order.

proof.text: The recovery test produces a report an auditor accepts as evidence
proof.how: Show the report to the customer's audit or compliance contact.

proof.text: An application and its database come back together, from the same moment, in the planned order
proof.how: Recover a grouped application in test mode and check its consistency and start order

readiness: Recovery point and time agreed for the workloads in the test
A target site or cloud with enough capacity for the test failover
An isolated test network so the failover does not touch production
Address, DNS and firewall changes for the recovery site listed
An administrator account to try to delete the copies with, agreed with security
Who starts the test, who watches it, and who signs the result

audiences.executive: Know how long the business can be down and how much data it can lose, and prove it recovers within that, ransomware included.
audiences.technical: Recovery objectives per application, protection by policy, dependent applications recovered together and in order, tested without touching production.
audiences.financial: Pay for the recovery each application needs, not the same for all; no full recovery site sitting idle at full cost.

people: The business owner who can put a number on a day down
The backup and recovery team
Security, for ransomware and copies that cannot be changed
Owners of the most critical applications
Audit or compliance, if recovery tests must be evidenced

objections.says: We already have backups.
objections.clarify: When did you last restore a whole application, and how long did it take?
objections.answer: Backups are copies; recovery is a tested time. Start from the time the business needs and test against it.
objections.prove: Restore a whole application in a test and time it against its agreed objective.

objections.says: A second site is too expensive.
objections.clarify: Which applications really need minutes, and which can wait hours?
objections.answer: Tier the applications: few need a standing copy elsewhere; the rest can recover from cheaper storage or a site that grows when needed.
objections.prove: Recover one application from each tier and record the time, and what keeping it ready costs.

objections.says: Testing recovery would disrupt production.
objections.clarify: What made past tests disruptive: the network, the people, the data?
objections.answer: Test on an isolated network, from copies, while production keeps running.
objections.prove: Run a test failover on an isolated network in working hours, with no impact on production.

objections.says: Ransomware would encrypt the backups too.
objections.clarify: Can an administrator account delete or change backups today?
objections.answer: Keep copies that nobody can change or delete for a set time, administrators included, and check they are clean before recovering.
objections.prove: Try to delete a locked copy with an administrator account, then recover from it.

dbaas.label: Databases as a service
dbaas.description: Database platform as a service: database environments whose provisioning, patching, backup, cloning and recovery are run by a platform instead of by hand.

questions.q: How long does a team wait today for a copy of production, and who makes it?
questions.why: Copy time is usually the most visible pain and the easiest win.
questions.need: A team gets a safe copy of production in under an hour
questions.how: Offer self-service clones from approved profiles
questions.listen: Days or weeks of waiting for a copy is lost development time: the figure is the value.
questions.probe: How many copies are requested each month, and how many are refused?

questions.q: When did you last restore a database to a precise point in time, and how long did it take?
questions.why: Untested point-in-time recovery is the usual hidden gap.
questions.need: Any database can be restored to a precise point in time, in a known time
questions.how: Restore one production database to a minute and time it
questions.listen: If nobody has done it recently, the recovery time is unknown.
questions.probe: What happens if wrong data is loaded at ten and found at eleven?

questions.q: How many databases are there, and how many does nobody own clearly?
questions.why: Databases outside any list are the ones that miss backups and patches.
questions.need: Every database is known and has an owner
questions.how: Register databases with the platform and assign owners
questions.listen: Databases with no clear owner are the ones that miss patches and backups.
questions.probe: How many database servers run a single small database?

questions.q: Which versions are you running, and how far are they from the supported ones?
questions.why: Version spread is effort and risk; it sizes the patching work.
questions.need: Database versions are within support
questions.how: Agree target versions and a patch window for the fleet
questions.listen: Versions out of support are a security and audit finding; upgrading them through automation is a strong case.
questions.probe: What stopped the last major version upgrade?

questions.q: Which production databases have no point-in-time backup today?
questions.why: The answer is the first list of the plan.
questions.need: Every production database has point-in-time backup
questions.how: Apply a backup policy to the databases without one
questions.listen: Production without point-in-time recovery means a logical error becomes lost data.
questions.probe: Which application owner believes they have it, and does not?

questions.q: How are test copies masked, if at all?
questions.why: Unmasked copies of production are a common data leak.
questions.need: Test copies are masked before a team sees them
questions.how: Mask sensitive columns as part of cloning
questions.listen: Personal data left unmasked in test is a compliance risk that automated copies can close.
questions.probe: Who checks that a test copy no longer holds personal data?

questions.q: Which databases must survive a server failure without anyone acting?
questions.why: Separates what needs a cluster from what does not.
questions.need: Databases that must survive a server failure do so with nobody acting
questions.how: Cluster the ones that need it, and test a failure
questions.listen: High availability built by hand differs from one database to the next; standard patterns cut the risk.
questions.probe: Which high-availability methods are used, and which licence level does each need?

questions.q: Who is woken up when a backup fails, and how quickly do they know?
questions.why: A failed backup nobody sees is no backup.
questions.need: A failed backup wakes the right person within minutes
questions.how: Route backup alerts to a named on-call owner
questions.listen: A failed backup found only on restore day is the classic failure.
questions.probe: When was a failed backup last discovered, and how late?

questions.q: Which database engines and editions run today, and how are they licensed: per core, per server, or by subscription?
questions.why: Engine and licence shape the platform, the hosts and the savings.
questions.need: Engines, editions and licence models are listed
questions.how: List every engine and edition with its licence model
questions.listen: Per-core licences reward fewer, faster cores on dedicated hosts: consolidation can pay for the project.
questions.probe: When is the next licence true-up or audit, and what did the last one find?

questions.q: How large is each important database, how fast does it grow, and how much of it is busy at any one time?
questions.why: The busy part belongs on the fastest storage; size and growth drive capacity.
questions.need: Size, growth and busy data are measured for the important databases
questions.how: Collect size, growth and an hour of peak activity for the top databases
questions.listen: When the busy part fits in the fastest tier, latency stays low: measure it rather than guess.
questions.probe: Which database has grown fastest, and why?

questions.q: What do the important databases ask of storage: transactions per second, latency, and when is the peak?
questions.why: Measured peaks size the platform and give the proof a target.
questions.need: Peak load and latency targets are known for each important database
questions.how: Pull a performance report covering the busiest hour
questions.listen: A latency target agreed now becomes a pass-or-fail line in the proof.
questions.probe: What does the application owner see when latency doubles?

questions.q: How long does a routine patch take per database, and how often is it skipped?
questions.why: Patching by hand is where database fleets fall behind.
questions.need: Patching time per database and the backlog are known
questions.how: Count the patches applied and skipped last quarter
questions.listen: If patching runs one server at a time at night, patching the whole fleet at once is the headline saving.
questions.probe: How many databases missed the last security patch, and why?

questions.q: Do developers get databases themselves today, or only through a ticket?
questions.why: Self-service within limits is the change the business notices.
questions.need: Developers get approved databases without a ticket
questions.how: Agree a catalogue of database sizes and versions developers may request
questions.listen: Tickets that take days push teams to cloud databases or to servers nobody knows about.
questions.probe: Which team has started using a cloud database to avoid waiting?

questions.q: Who owns database standards (versions, sizes, backup policies), and how are they enforced?
questions.why: Standards held in a document drift; standards built into templates hold.
questions.need: Database standards are written down and applied by templates
questions.how: List the standards and check how many databases follow them
questions.listen: Standards that live only on a wiki are ignored under pressure.
questions.probe: What share of databases follow the backup standard today?

proof.text: A production database is restored to a point in time five minutes before a simulated error, within the agreed time
proof.how: Drop a table on a copy of production, restore to the minute before, and time it end to end.

proof.text: A masked copy of a production database is delivered to a development team in under an hour, with no DBA ticket
proof.how: Have one team request a clone through self-service and check that sensitive columns are masked.

proof.text: The whole fleet moves to an approved patch level in one maintenance window, with a tested rollback
proof.how: Patch a group of test databases together, then roll one back.

proof.text: A new database is provisioned from an approved profile in minutes, with backup already on
proof.how: Request one, then check its backup policy without touching it.

proof.text: A database server failure leaves the clustered database available with no manual step
proof.how: Stop the primary node during a test load and watch the service continue.

readiness: A copy of a production database cleared for the test, or a representative one
Database engine versions and licences in scope listed
A DBA and an application team ready to try self-service
The columns to mask agreed with the data owner
Backup target and retention for the test

audiences.executive: Databases delivered in minutes to the teams that need them, protected and patched to one standard.
audiences.technical: Provisioning, cloning, patching and point-in-time recovery for each engine, as self-service within guardrails.
audiences.financial: Fewer full copies of production data, licences counted where databases actually run, less DBA time on routine work.

people: The DBA team lead
Development teams asking for databases
Security, for masked copies of production data
Licensing, for database licences

objections.says: Our DBAs will not give up control.
objections.clarify: Which tasks do they want to keep, and which take their time today?
objections.answer: They set the standards and approve; routine provisioning, patching and cloning become self-service within those standards.
objections.prove: A developer gets a masked copy of a production database in minutes, under a policy the DBAs set.

objections.says: Our databases are too critical to move.
objections.clarify: Which ones, on which engines and versions, and with which recovery objective?
objections.answer: Start with test and development copies, then the less critical, with recovery tested at each step.
objections.prove: Restore a database to a point in time chosen by the DBA, and check it.

objections.says: We would need new licences.
objections.clarify: How are database licences counted today, and on how many cores?
objections.answer: Count licences against where databases will run; consolidating can reduce the cores to license.
objections.prove: Compare the cores the databases need on the new platform with the cores licensed today.

object-storage.label: Object storage
object-storage.description: S3-compatible object storage: tenants that keep buckets for applications, backups and archives, with immutability, replication, encryption and access to adopt.

questions.q: What data would hurt most if it were encrypted or deleted tomorrow?
questions.why: Points straight at the buckets that need immutability first.
questions.need: The data that would hurt most is known and protected first
questions.how: Name it with the business, and protect it first
questions.listen: Backups and records under legal hold usually top the list; they set the level of protection.
questions.probe: Which of that data has a legal retention period?

questions.q: What do you pay today per terabyte, including egress and requests?
questions.why: Request and egress fees are where storage bills surprise people.
questions.need: The full cost per terabyte is known
questions.how: Add up storage, egress and requests for a typical month
questions.listen: Charges for retrieval and requests often double the headline price.
questions.probe: What did retrieving data cost the last time you restored from the cloud?

questions.q: Which applications and backup jobs write to object storage, and where?
questions.why: Unknown writers mean unknown tenants and keys.
questions.need: Every application and backup job writing to object storage is known
questions.how: List writers and their buckets
questions.listen: Each application that writes is a compatibility test for the proof.
questions.probe: Which of them use more than simple reads and writes: versioning, lifecycle rules, notifications?

questions.q: Do you know how many access keys exist, who owns them and when they were last used?
questions.why: Old keys with broad rights are the easiest way in.
questions.need: Every access key has an owner and is used
questions.how: Review keys, give owners, and remove unused ones
questions.listen: Old keys with broad rights are a common way in.
questions.probe: When was a key last rotated, and what broke?

questions.q: Are your backup copies under object lock, and for how long?
questions.why: Backups an administrator can delete do not survive ransomware.
questions.need: Backup copies are under object lock for long enough
questions.how: Turn on object lock with the agreed retention
questions.listen: Backups that can be deleted with the right keys can be deleted by an attacker.
questions.probe: Which lock mode is used: one even administrators cannot override, or one they can?

questions.q: Must any data stay in a given country, and can you prove where it is?
questions.why: Residency is often a legal requirement before it is a technical one.
questions.need: Data that must stay in a country stays there, with proof
questions.how: Pin buckets to regions and keep the evidence
questions.listen: Being able to prove where data is matters as much as where it is.
questions.probe: Who would ask for that proof: a regulator, a customer, an auditor?

questions.q: When did you last restore from these backups, and how long did it take?
questions.why: The restore is the only test that counts.
questions.need: A restore from object storage has been tested and timed
questions.how: Restore one backup end to end and time it
questions.listen: Restore speed depends on throughput, not capacity: measure it.
questions.probe: How long would restoring the largest system from these copies take?

questions.q: Who is alerted when someone reads or deletes far more than usual?
questions.why: Mass reads and deletes are the first signs of theft or ransomware.
questions.need: Unusual reads or deletes alert someone named
questions.how: Alert on unusual volumes, routed to an owner
questions.listen: Mass reads can mean theft; mass deletes can mean an attack.
questions.probe: Who can stop a key from working within minutes?

questions.q: How much data will be stored, in how many objects, and how much is written each day?
questions.why: Capacity, object count and daily writes size the platform.
questions.need: Capacity, object count and daily writes are estimated
questions.how: Collect current size and daily writes per bucket or application
questions.listen: Billions of small objects stress metadata more than capacity: ask about object size too.
questions.probe: What is the typical object size, and the largest?

questions.q: How fast must data be written and read back, in the backup window and during a restore?
questions.why: Throughput, not capacity, decides backup and restore times.
questions.need: The throughput needed for backup and restore is known
questions.how: Divide the size of the backup set by its window to get the throughput needed
questions.listen: A nightly window and a restore target give a throughput the design must meet.
questions.probe: What is the restore time target for the largest backup set?

questions.q: Which data should move to cheaper storage, or be deleted, automatically as it ages?
questions.why: Lifecycle rules keep cost down without anyone acting.
questions.need: Lifecycle and retention rules are agreed per data set
questions.how: Agree tiering and expiry per bucket with its owner
questions.listen: Data kept forever by default is the cost to cut: give each rule an owner.
questions.probe: Which data set has no retention rule at all today?

questions.q: Do analytics or AI teams need to read this data where it is, and with which tools?
questions.why: Data read in place avoids copies and transfer charges.
questions.need: Needs to read data in place for analytics or AI are known
questions.how: Ask the data teams which tools and protocols they would read with
questions.listen: Reading in place turns a backup target into a data platform: a strong second use.
questions.probe: How much data is copied today only to be analysed elsewhere?

questions.q: Will the storage serve several teams or customers, each seeing only its own data and usage?
questions.why: Serving several tenants needs isolation, quotas and usage per tenant.
questions.need: Tenants, quotas and usage reporting are agreed
questions.how: List the teams or customers and what each must see
questions.listen: Charging back per team needs usage per tenant from the first day.
questions.probe: How is the cost of storage split between teams today?

questions.q: How would you know if a bucket were open to the internet, and who checks?
questions.why: An open bucket is one of the most common ways data leaks.
questions.need: No bucket is open to the internet by mistake, and a change that opens one is caught
questions.how: List the buckets that are public on purpose, and alert on any other that becomes public
questions.listen: A list of the public ones and an alert; "nobody would do that" is what every leak report starts with.
questions.probe: Which buckets are public on purpose today, and who decided?

proof.text: An object under object lock cannot be deleted or overwritten, even with administrator credentials, until its retention ends
proof.how: Write a test object with a retention date, then try to delete it as the bucket owner and as an administrator.

proof.text: A backup job writes to the bucket and a full restore of a test system completes within the agreed time
proof.how: Run the customer's own backup software against the bucket and time a restore of one system.

proof.text: Losing one site or node leaves every object readable, with no manual step
proof.how: Take one site or node offline during reads and check that every object still returns.

proof.text: Data stays in the countries the policy names, and the placement can be shown to an auditor
proof.how: Write objects under a residency policy and export where each copy lives.

proof.text: The customer's existing S3 tools and applications work unchanged against the endpoint
proof.how: Point two real applications and one command-line tool at the endpoint and run their normal jobs.

proof.text: The monthly cost for the customer's real volume and access pattern is known before signature, egress and requests included
proof.how: Replay a month of the customer's usage figures through the price list and agree the total with finance.

readiness: A test bucket and the application or backup job that will write to it
Object lock retention for the test agreed
Network path and throughput between writers and the storage
The residency rule for the test data
A restore to time, with its target agreed

audiences.executive: Backups and records that must not change kept safe from deletion, at low cost, in the country you choose.
audiences.technical: S3-compatible buckets with object lock, replication, tenants and encryption keys under your control.
audiences.financial: Cheaper per terabyte than block or file for backups and archives, with no charge for reading back data kept on premises.

people: The backup owner
Application teams that write to S3
Security, for keys and immutability
Compliance, for retention rules

objections.says: We will just use a public cloud bucket.
objections.clarify: How much is read back each month, and must the data stay in the country?
objections.answer: Compare the total, including reads and transfer out, and where the data must live.
objections.prove: Model the monthly cost of the test dataset, read-back included, here and in a public bucket.

objections.says: On premises, an administrator can always delete.
objections.clarify: Who can delete today, and what would an auditor accept as proof?
objections.answer: Use a retention lock that no account can lift before it expires, and show it.
objections.prove: Try to delete a locked object with the most powerful administrator account.

objections.says: Our backup software may not support it.
objections.clarify: Which product and version, and which features: lock, tiering?
objections.answer: Check the compatibility of the exact versions in use, and test them.
objections.prove: Run a backup and a restore with the customer's own backup software against a locked bucket.

edge-sites.label: Edge and branch sites
edge-sites.description: Edge and branch sites: small clusters in shops, plants, branches and remote locations, deployed without local IT, managed and upgraded centrally, protected locally and at the core, and running local applications, AI included.

questions.q: What happens to the business at a site when its systems stop: a till, a production line, a branch counter?
questions.why: The cost of a site stopping decides how much resilience each kind of site needs.
questions.need: The cost of a site stopping is known per kind of site
questions.how: Put a figure on an hour of downtime for each kind of site
questions.listen: Sites where a stop halts sales or production justify two servers and local recovery; others can live with one.
questions.probe: Which site stopped last, for how long, and what did it cost?

questions.q: How often does someone travel to a site to fix, replace or upgrade something, and what does a visit cost?
questions.why: Site visits are the hidden cost of distributed infrastructure.
questions.need: Site visits and their cost are counted
questions.how: Count last year's visits and their reasons
questions.listen: Visits for routine upgrades or disk swaps are what central management removes.
questions.probe: Which visit could have been done remotely if the tools allowed it?

questions.q: How many sites are there, of how many kinds, and what runs at each?
questions.why: Kinds of site, not their number, decide the standard designs.
questions.need: Sites are grouped into a few standard kinds
questions.how: List sites with their applications and size
questions.listen: Three or four standard site designs make hundreds of sites manageable; one design per site does not.
questions.probe: Which site is the exception everyone remembers, and why?

questions.q: What network connects each site: bandwidth, latency, and how often does it drop?
questions.why: The link decides what runs locally, how copies travel and how upgrades arrive.
questions.need: Bandwidth, latency and outages are known per kind of site
questions.how: Collect link speeds and last quarter's outages
questions.listen: Sites that lose their link must keep working alone, then catch up; plan for both.
questions.probe: What must keep working at a site when its link is down for a day?

questions.q: How old is the hardware at the sites, and when does its support end?
questions.why: A refresh across many sites is a date and a budget.
questions.need: Site hardware is listed with its support dates
questions.how: Export the site hardware list with purchase dates
questions.listen: A wave of sites going out of support is the reason to standardise now.
questions.probe: How many sites go out of support next year?

questions.q: Who can see, from one place, the health of every site right now?
questions.why: Without a central view, problems are found by the people at the site.
questions.need: Every site's health is visible centrally
questions.how: Bring one region's sites under one view
questions.listen: Problems reported by shop or plant staff mean the central view is missing.
questions.probe: How did you learn about the last site problem: an alert, or a phone call?

questions.q: Who looks after the sites day to day: a central team, local staff, or a partner?
questions.why: Who operates the sites decides how much must be automatic.
questions.need: The operating model for the sites is agreed
questions.how: Map who does what at the sites today
questions.listen: Sites run by people who are not in IT need everything remote and simple; partners need clear boundaries.
questions.probe: What do local staff do today that they should not have to?

questions.q: Which sites must keep running if one server fails, and which can wait for a replacement?
questions.why: One-server sites cost less; two or three servers keep running through a failure.
questions.need: Each kind of site has an agreed tolerance to a server failure
questions.how: Agree a tolerance per kind of site with the business
questions.listen: Two-server sites need a small witness elsewhere to decide which side keeps running: ask where it would live.
questions.probe: Where could a small witness service run that every site can reach?

questions.q: How are sites backed up today, and how long would restoring a site take without its link?
questions.why: A copy that exists only at the core is slow to bring back over a thin link.
questions.need: Each site has a local copy and a copy at the core
questions.how: Time a restore of one site's main application
questions.listen: Restores over a thin link take days; a local copy brings a site back in minutes.
questions.probe: What is the largest site, and how long would its data take to copy back?

questions.q: How are upgrades done across the sites today, and how far behind are the oldest?
questions.why: Sites left on old versions are where security holes stay open.
questions.need: Sites are upgraded remotely, in waves
questions.how: List the versions running across the sites
questions.listen: Sites several versions behind are an audit finding waiting to happen; remote, staged upgrades are the answer.
questions.probe: How long did the last upgrade campaign take to reach every site?

questions.q: Who can physically reach the servers at a site, and are their disks encrypted?
questions.why: Servers in shops and plants can be stolen or tampered with.
questions.need: Site servers are encrypted and locked down by default
questions.how: Check encryption and physical access at three sites
questions.listen: Unencrypted disks in a back office become a data breach the day they are stolen.
questions.probe: What would be exposed if the server at your smallest site walked out of the door?

questions.q: Which new applications should run at the sites: cameras, quality inspection, local AI, sensors?
questions.why: New applications at the edge decide the next design, and whether it needs GPUs.
questions.need: Planned edge applications are listed with their needs
questions.how: List applications planned for the sites in the next two years
questions.listen: Video and AI at the edge need GPUs and storage at the site; data that cannot leave the site settles where it runs.
questions.probe: Which data from the sites can never leave them, and why?

questions.q: How is a new site opened today, and how long until its systems run?
questions.why: Opening sites quickly is a business goal in retail and manufacturing.
questions.need: A new site runs from a standard design within days
questions.how: Time the last site opening from delivery to running
questions.listen: Weeks to open a site point to manual builds; standard designs deployed remotely cut it to days.
questions.probe: How many sites will open next year?

questions.q: Which applications must keep working at a site when its network link is down, and for how long?
questions.why: A site that depends on the link stops when the link does, whatever runs locally.
questions.need: The applications that matter keep working at a site without its link, for as long as the business needs
questions.how: List per kind of site what must work offline and for how long, and test one site with its link cut
questions.listen: A clear list with hours; "everything is in the cloud now" means a link failure stops the site.
questions.probe: When did a site last lose its link, and what stopped while it was down?

proof.text: A new site is deployed from a standard design with no IT staff on site
proof.how: Ship a test site and have it join the central plane from the network alone

proof.text: Every test site is seen and upgraded from one place, in waves, without a visit
proof.how: Upgrade the test sites in two waves and record any visit needed

proof.text: A site keeps running when one server fails, and the people working there do not notice
proof.how: Power off a server at a two-server test site during a simulated working day

proof.text: A site's main application is restored from a local copy with the link down
proof.how: Cut the link, delete a test machine and restore it locally

proof.text: Each site's workloads reach the core within the agreed recovery point, over the real link
proof.how: Measure replication lag over a week on the real link

proof.text: An inference application runs at the site on local data that never leaves it
proof.how: Run a sample model on local images and confirm nothing is sent out

readiness: Two or three test sites chosen, one of each kind
Network details for each test site: addresses, link speed, firewall rules to the core
Somewhere to run a witness, reachable from the two-server sites
A core site or cloud to replicate to
Someone at each test site who can plug in a server, and nothing more
The business agrees a window for the failure test

audiences.executive: Open and run sites without sending IT: standard designs deployed remotely, every site upgraded from one place, and a site that keeps working when a server fails.
audiences.technical: Small clusters from one server to a few, deployed without hands on site, upgraded remotely in waves, with local copies plus replication to the core, encrypted by default, and room for AI at the edge.
audiences.financial: Fewer site visits and emergency replacements; one standard design bought in volume instead of a different one per site.

people: The head of stores, plants or branches
Infrastructure operations for the sites
Security, for equipment outside the data centre
Whoever installs equipment at the sites, staff or partner

objections.says: Our sites are too small for this.
objections.clarify: What runs at your smallest site, and what happens when it stops?
objections.answer: One server where a stop can wait, two where it cannot; both managed from the same place as the rest.
objections.prove: Run the smallest site's applications on a one-server test site managed centrally.

objections.says: The links to our sites are too poor.
objections.clarify: Which sites lose their link, and for how long?
objections.answer: Sites keep working alone and catch up when the link returns; upgrades and copies are scheduled around the link.
objections.prove: Cut a test site's link for a working day and show it runs and catches up.

objections.says: We cannot send people to install servers everywhere.
objections.clarify: Who is at the sites today who could plug in a box?
objections.answer: Servers ship configured and join the central plane on their own; nobody with IT skills needs to travel.
objections.prove: Ship a server to a test site and have someone outside IT plug it in.

objections.says: AI at the edge is not for us yet.
objections.clarify: Is there data at the sites, like images or sensor readings, that nobody looks at?
objections.answer: Size the sites so a GPU can be added later; start with the applications that run there today.
objections.prove: Show the site design with room for a GPU, and its cost now and later.

cloud-operations.label: Cloud operations and self-service
cloud-operations.description: Cloud operations on private infrastructure: capacity planned before it runs out, routine work automated, a self-service catalog with guardrails, costs shown per team, and security posture checked against a baseline.

questions.q: How many hours a month go into routine operations: provisioning, patching, capacity checks, reports?
questions.why: Hours of routine work are what automation gives back, in the team's own count.
questions.need: Routine hours are counted per task
questions.how: List the routine tasks of a month with their hours
questions.listen: A team that cannot count its routine hours spends more than it thinks: count three tasks with them.
questions.probe: Which task would you hand to a machine first, and why that one?

questions.q: How long does a team wait for a new machine, environment or database, from request to use?
questions.why: Waiting time is the delay the business feels, and why teams go around IT.
questions.need: The wait from request to use is measured
questions.how: Time the last five requests from ticket to use
questions.listen: Days or weeks of waiting push teams to the public cloud or to machines nobody manages.
questions.probe: What did the last team that could not wait do instead?

questions.q: How many sites and clusters are managed today, and from how many separate consoles?
questions.why: Every extra console is another place to check and another skill to keep.
questions.need: All sites and clusters are listed with the tool that manages each
questions.how: List sites and clusters with their management tool
questions.listen: Several consoles for one estate means nobody sees the whole: one plane is the first win.
questions.probe: Which site was last checked by hand, and when?

questions.q: When will the busiest cluster run out of processor, memory or storage, and who would notice first?
questions.why: Capacity that runs out unannounced becomes an emergency purchase.
questions.need: Each cluster has a forecast with a run-out date
questions.how: Forecast growth from three months of usage
questions.listen: If the answer is 'when users complain', capacity is managed by incident; a forecast with a date changes the budget conversation.
questions.probe: When did you last buy hardware in a hurry, and what did it cost?

questions.q: How do you find out that an application is slower than usual before its users do?
questions.why: Problems found by users cost more than problems found by monitoring.
questions.need: Unusual behaviour raises an alert before users notice
questions.how: Compare the last incident's first alert with its first complaint
questions.listen: Fixed thresholds miss slow drifts; baselines learned from the system's own behaviour catch them earlier.
questions.probe: What was the last problem users reported before any alert fired?

questions.q: How many machines are oversized, idle or forgotten, and what do they hold?
questions.why: Reclaiming waste is the cheapest capacity there is.
questions.need: Idle and oversized machines are listed with an owner's decision
questions.how: List machines idle for a month or using under a fifth of what they have
questions.listen: Most estates hold a fifth or more of waste; reclaiming it postpones the next purchase.
questions.probe: Who can decide to shrink or switch off a machine that belongs to another team?

questions.q: Do the public cloud bills and the data-centre costs end up in the same view, on the same basis?
questions.why: Choosing where to run something needs costs compared like for like.
questions.need: Private and public cloud costs are seen side by side
questions.how: Put last quarter's cloud bill next to the data-centre cost per machine
questions.listen: Two views on two bases lead to wrong placement decisions, in both directions.
questions.probe: Which workload would you move if you saw both costs side by side?

questions.q: Which routine tasks are scripted today, who maintains the scripts, and what happens when that person is away?
questions.why: Scripts in one person's folder are a risk, not automation.
questions.need: Routine tasks run as shared, maintained runbooks
questions.how: List the scripts in use with their owner and last change
questions.listen: Scripts kept by one person are a single point of failure; shared runbooks with approvals and logs are the step up.
questions.probe: Which script would stop working if its author left tomorrow?

questions.q: Can teams order standard services themselves, with approvals and quotas, or does every request go through a ticket?
questions.why: Self-service within limits is how a private estate competes with the public cloud.
questions.need: Teams order approved services from a catalog within quotas
questions.how: Turn three frequent requests into catalog items
questions.listen: Tickets for standard requests mean the catalog is the gap; quotas and approvals answer the fear of sprawl.
questions.probe: Which request is asked for most often, and how standard is it really?

questions.q: Is each team shown what its infrastructure costs, and are those costs charged back?
questions.why: Without a cost per team, demand grows without limit and the platform looks expensive.
questions.need: Cost per team or project is shown back or charged back
questions.how: Agree a cost per machine and allocate last month's estate to teams
questions.listen: A unit cost per machine, built from hardware, licences, power, space and people, settles 'the cloud is cheaper' with facts.
questions.probe: What does one virtual machine cost you a month, all in?

questions.q: How is the estate checked against security baselines and regulations, and how often?
questions.why: Configuration drifts between audits; continuous checks catch it.
questions.need: Security posture is checked continuously against a baseline
questions.how: Pick a baseline and run a first check across the estate
questions.listen: A yearly audit by spreadsheet means months of drift; continuous checks with a report the auditor accepts are the change.
questions.probe: What did the last audit find that had changed since the one before?

questions.q: Must the management plane and its data stay on your own premises, or may it run as a hosted service?
questions.why: Sovereignty rules can forbid management and monitoring data leaving the country.
questions.need: Management and its data run where the rules require
questions.how: Ask security where management and monitoring data may live
questions.listen: Regulated customers often need the management plane itself on premises: ask before proposing a hosted service.
questions.probe: Who approved the current monitoring tools from a data-protection point of view?

questions.q: Who reviews capacity, cost and compliance each month, and what decisions come out of it?
questions.why: Reports nobody acts on are noise.
questions.need: A monthly review decides on capacity, cost and compliance
questions.how: Set up a monthly review with an owner and a short agenda
questions.listen: A review that ends in decisions turns data into budget and priorities.
questions.probe: What was the last decision taken because of a capacity or cost report?

questions.q: Which approvals are needed before a change or a new service, and how long do they take?
questions.why: Approvals built into the request are faster than approvals by email.
questions.need: Approvals run inside the request, with a time limit
questions.how: Map the approval steps for one common request
questions.listen: Approvals by email add days; the same rules inside the workflow keep control without the wait.
questions.probe: Which approval is given every time, and could become automatic?

proof.text: A capacity forecast names the cluster that runs out first, and when, from the customer's own usage
proof.how: Collect a month of usage and compare the forecast with the team's own estimate

proof.text: A routine task the team does by hand runs as an automated runbook, with approval and a log
proof.how: Automate the most frequent manual task end to end and read its log

proof.text: A team orders a standard environment from a catalog and gets it within the agreed time, inside its quota
proof.how: Publish one catalog item with a quota and time a request from a real team

proof.text: Last month's cost is allocated to teams on a cost per machine agreed with finance
proof.how: Build the cost model with finance and allocate one month

proof.text: A baseline check finds a real drift, and security accepts the report
proof.how: Run the baseline across the estate and review the findings with security

proof.text: An unusual slowdown raises an alert before the application owner notices
proof.how: Load a test machine until it slows and see who is told first

readiness: The sites and clusters in scope, with read access for the management plane
A month of usage data, or the time to collect it
Three frequent requests chosen to become catalog items, with their owners
Finance agrees the cost elements: hardware, licences, power, space, people
The security baseline to check against, chosen by security
A test team willing to order through the catalog

audiences.executive: Run your own infrastructure like a cloud: teams served in minutes, costs visible per team, and compliance shown continuously instead of once a year.
audiences.technical: One management plane for every site: capacity forecasts with dates, alerts on unusual behaviour, runbooks instead of scripts, a catalog with quotas and approvals, posture checked against a baseline.
audiences.financial: Reclaim idle capacity before buying more, show each team what it costs, and compare private and public cloud on the same basis.

people: The head of infrastructure operations
Application teams that request environments
Finance, or whoever leads cloud cost management
Security and compliance

objections.says: We already have monitoring tools.
objections.clarify: Do they forecast when capacity runs out, and act on what they find, or only draw graphs?
objections.answer: Keep what works; add forecasts with dates and runbooks that act, on one plane for every site.
objections.prove: Forecast the busiest cluster's run-out date and automate the fix for its most frequent alert.

objections.says: Self-service will create sprawl.
objections.clarify: What sprawl did you see the last time teams had access: size, number, or machines nobody claimed?
objections.answer: Catalog items come with quotas, approvals and an expiry, so self-service is faster and tidier than tickets.
objections.prove: Publish one catalog item with a quota and an expiry, and show what happens when the quota is reached.

objections.says: Chargeback will start a political fight.
objections.clarify: Would showing costs first, without charging them, be accepted?
objections.answer: Start with showback on an agreed unit cost; charge back only once teams trust the numbers.
objections.prove: Show one month of cost per team to two team leads and ask whether the numbers look right.

objections.says: Automation will break production.
objections.clarify: Which change went wrong last time, and was it made by hand?
objections.answer: Runbooks run with approvals, logs and a dry run; they make the same change the same way every time.
objections.prove: Run one runbook as a dry run, approve it, run it, and read the log.

infrastructure.name: Renew the current platform
infrastructure.why: No migration, skills already in place, and a renewal is one signature away.
ask: What does the renewal cost against the last one, and for how long is that price fixed?
Which products in the renewal do you pay for and not use?
infrastructure.fits_us: The renewal costs much more than the last, bundles products nobody asked for, or locks the price for a short time only.
infrastructure.fits_them: The renewal is affordable and the team has no room for a move this year: plan for the renewal after, and keep the conversation open.
infrastructure.prove: The case for change month by month, and a test wave moved and rolled back.

infrastructure.name: Move everything to a public cloud
infrastructure.why: No hardware to buy or run, capacity on demand, and often a mandate from the board.
ask: Which workloads run at the same load all year round?
Does the cloud estimate include storage, backup, traffic out and support?
infrastructure.fits_us: Steady workloads, data that must stay in the country or close to plants and shops, and costs that grow with every machine left running.
infrastructure.fits_them: Workloads with sharp peaks, applications rebuilt for the cloud, or no data centre left to run: there the public cloud is the better home.
infrastructure.prove: What one machine costs here, side by side with the cloud, and the same platform running in the cloud for what belongs there.

infrastructure.name: Another hyperconverged or private-cloud platform
infrastructure.why: The same promise of simplicity, sometimes bundled with hardware or software the customer already buys.
ask: Which hardware and hypervisors does it support, and does choosing it lock either?
How is an upgrade of the whole stack done, and how long does it take?
infrastructure.fits_us: The customer wants freedom of hardware, one-step upgrades of the whole stack, and the same platform at the core, the edge and in the cloud.
infrastructure.fits_them: The customer has standardised on that vendor's hardware and tools, and its limits do not matter for the workloads in scope.
infrastructure.prove: Upgrades and failures tested during the proof of value, on the customer's chosen hardware.

infrastructure.name: Separate servers and storage arrays
infrastructure.why: Familiar, an array bought recently, and a feeling that separate parts perform better.
ask: When do the array and the servers go out of support, and what does the refresh cost?
How many teams and tools does it take to give an application a new machine with storage?
infrastructure.fits_us: The array or the servers are near the end of their support, and several teams have to agree every change.
infrastructure.fits_them: A large array bought recently with years of support left: start where it ends, or with workloads it does not serve.
infrastructure.prove: A performance test on the customer's own workload, and the time to deliver a machine end to end.

infrastructure.name: Build it with open-source virtualisation
infrastructure.why: No licence fees, full control, and engineers keen to build it.
ask: Who answers a failure at three in the morning, and within what time?
How many people would build, upgrade and secure it, and for how many years?
infrastructure.fits_us: The team is small, uptime matters, and the people who would build it are needed elsewhere.
infrastructure.fits_them: A large engineering team that already runs open-source infrastructure at scale and wants to own every layer.
infrastructure.prove: The cost per machine with the people counted, and a support case opened and solved during the proof of value.

infrastructure.name: Do nothing for now
infrastructure.why: No budget this year, other priorities, and nothing seems broken.
ask: What happens on the contract end date if nothing changes?
What did the last outage or the last emergency purchase cost?
infrastructure.fits_us: A date that cannot move: a contract end, hardware out of support, an audit, a regulation.
infrastructure.fits_them: No date and no pain the customer can name: agree what would make it urgent, and when to talk again.
infrastructure.prove: The cost of waiting, month by month, and a first step small enough to fit this year's budget.

dr-backup.name: Keep the backup product you have
dr-backup.why: It runs, people know it, and the contract is paid.
ask: When did you last restore a whole application from it, and how long did it take?
Could an administrator, or an attacker with their account, delete the copies?
dr-backup.fits_us: Restores take too long, copies can be deleted, or recovering a whole site has never been tested.
dr-backup.fits_them: Restores are tested and fast and the copies are already immutable: add recovery plans, not a new backup product.
dr-backup.prove: A whole application restored and timed, and a delete refused on an immutable copy.

dr-backup.name: Recovery as a service from a provider
dr-backup.why: No second site to build, equip or staff.
ask: What recovery time does the provider commit to, and how is it tested?
Where would the copies live, and who could reach them?
dr-backup.fits_us: Recovery in under an hour, data that must stay in the country, or a second site already owned.
dr-backup.fits_them: No second site, modest recovery times and a provider with tested runbooks: it can be the simpler choice.
dr-backup.prove: A test failover timed against the recovery time the provider would commit to.

object-storage.name: Object storage in a public cloud
object-storage.why: Capacity without limit, and nothing to run.
ask: How much data is read back each month, and what do reads and traffic out cost?
Must the copies stay in the country, under whose keys?
object-storage.fits_us: Large, steady capacity read back often, data that must stay on premises, or restores needed at local speed.
object-storage.fits_them: Small or cold archives rarely read back, with no residency rule: the public cloud is cheaper there.
object-storage.prove: The cost per TiB a year with reads and traffic counted, and a restore at local speed.

object-storage.name: A dedicated backup appliance
object-storage.why: One box from the backup vendor, one support line.
ask: Can it keep copies nobody can delete for the whole retention?
What happens when it is full: another box?
object-storage.fits_us: Backups from several products, growth beyond one box, or object lock needed by several applications.
object-storage.fits_them: One backup product, a steady size, and a team that wants a single vendor.
object-storage.prove: Object lock tested with an administrator account, and capacity added without a new box.

dbaas.name: Managed databases in a public cloud
dbaas.why: Patching, backups and copies done by the provider.
ask: Which databases sit next to applications that stay on premises?
What would the same database cost there, with its storage and licences?
dbaas.fits_us: Databases close to applications on premises, licences already owned, or data that must stay.
dbaas.fits_them: New applications built in the cloud, with their data there: a managed database there is natural.
dbaas.prove: A copy delivered in minutes on premises, and the cost per database side by side.

dbaas.name: Keep doing it with scripts and the DBA team
dbaas.why: The DBAs know the databases, and the scripts work.
ask: How long does a developer wait for a copy of production?
When was each database last patched, and last restored to a point in time?
dbaas.fits_us: Developers waiting days for copies, patches months behind, restores never tested.
dbaas.fits_them: Few databases, a strong DBA team, and copies already delivered fast.
dbaas.prove: A masked copy delivered on request, and a point-in-time restore timed.

cloud-operations.name: The monitoring tools already in place, plus scripts
cloud-operations.why: Paid for, and the team knows them.
ask: Which of them says when capacity will run out?
Who maintains the scripts, and what happens when that person is away?
cloud-operations.fits_us: No forecasts, scripts kept by one person, and a ticket for every standard request.
cloud-operations.fits_them: A small estate with few requests: better scripts may be enough.
cloud-operations.prove: A run-out date forecast, and a runbook replacing a script.

edge-sites.name: A server per site, as today
ask: What happens at a site when that server fails?
How many trips did upgrades and repairs take last year?
edge-sites.fits_us: Sites that cannot stop, many trips, upgrades behind.
edge-sites.fits_them: Sites that can wait a day for a replacement, with few applications: keep one server, managed centrally.
edge-sites.prove: A server failure at a two-server site, and an upgrade without a trip.

edge-sites.name: Run the sites from the cloud
edge-sites.why: No servers at the sites at all.
ask: What must keep working when a site's link is down?
How much data do cameras, tills or machines produce at the site?
edge-sites.fits_us: Links that drop, heavy local data, or tills and lines that cannot stop.
edge-sites.fits_them: Sites with reliable links that only run office applications.
edge-sites.prove: A site working through a day with its link cut.

any.topic: Data kept in the country or the EU
